_README: 🔴 THIS FILE IS A FEATURE, NOT A BACKLOG. Dr. John Phillips (Senior Advisor on Health Economic Research, Office of the NIH Director) told this cohort that lost productivity and caregiver time are 'really important... but they're also ones that are difficult to capture and difficult to measure,' and then asked teams to name the source. Naming honestly that no defensible federal figure exists is a better answer than producing one. The app renders these on the page, in the ledger, beside the priced lines.

items.label: Days of work you missed
items.whyUnpriced: Valuing a lost workday requires your actual earnings, not a national median. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes median usual weekly earnings for full-time wage and salary workers, but applying that median to a specific person is a guess about that person's pay, and it silently excludes part-time workers, the self-employed, and anyone who had already stopped working because of the illness — which is a large share of the people this tool exists for.
items.whatWouldFixIt: Ask the person for their own hourly or weekly pay and multiply. That is arithmetic on a figure they supplied, not an estimate we invented. The workdays card does this: it opens on the published national median with the division shown on its face, one tap switches it to your own weekly pay or blanks the line, and the result is never added to the medical total.

items.label: Time someone spent caring for you
items.whyUnpriced: There is no federal price for unpaid family caregiving. The standard workarounds — a replacement-wage approach using the home health aide occupational wage, or an opportunity-cost approach using the caregiver's own foregone earnings — give materially different answers and neither is a published federal figure for this purpose. Choosing one silently would be choosing the answer.
items.whatWouldFixIt: State the method and let the reader pick it, showing the numbers side by side rather than one. The unpaid-care card does this: four published BLS rates, from $17.21 an hour for custodial help to $46.90 for nursing-level care, each with its arithmetic, none of them added to the medical total.

items.label: Travel to appointments
items.whyUnpriced: Mileage rates exist — the IRS publishes a medical mileage rate — but the distance travelled is specific to a person and their geography, and rural patients routinely travel an order of magnitude further than urban ones. A national average here would be wrong for exactly the people it matters most to.
items.whatWouldFixIt: Ask for the round-trip distance and apply a published federal rate. The table carries one: the GSA privately-owned-vehicle rate, $0.76 a mile effective 1 July 2026 — what the government reimburses its own travellers for a mile, which is not a medical price and is never added to a medical total. The IRS medical mileage rate is the other published choice. Real input, published rate, honest arithmetic.

items.label: What YOU paid, as opposed to what your insurer paid
items.whyUnpriced: Federal expenditure files report what was spent in total, every payer combined, and splitting that into 'yours' and 'theirs' without a published split would be inventing the most personally meaningful number on the page. The one national estimate that did test the split found no significant difference: $236 a year more out of pocket for adults reporting long COVID, on an interval running from minus $95 to plus $566, p = 0.162.
items.whatWouldFixIt: A published out-of-pocket split for the care actually in your ledger. None exists. The tool says 'not reported' rather than guessing, and shows the one tested national estimate with its interval, which crosses zero.

items.label: What the delay itself cost you
items.whyUnpriced: This is a causal claim — that being diagnosed later produced worse outcomes and higher costs than being diagnosed sooner — and it needs an identification strategy, not a price. Without a design that separates the effect of the delay from the effect of being sicker in the first place, any number here is a correlation dressed as a cost.
items.whatWouldFixIt: A study design. Until there is one, this line is named on the page and left blank, because the cost is real even though the figure is not available.
